title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: Major stuffed with equivocations — sine quo as condition vs means; elect infants
pass_a_gloss: But let us ventilate the syllogism itself. The Major proposition, Without that without which it is impossible to please God, without it it is impossible that anyone be elected to salvation, is wholly stuffed with equivocations. Those words, without which, can be understood doubly: without which, foreseen and preconsidered as an antecedent condition, no one can be elected to salvation by God; or, without which as a prepared and destined means it is impossible that anyone be elected to salvation. In the prior sense it touches the cause, but is manifestly false: In the latter it does not even touch it, and yet is not of absolute truth. For indeed they so far please God that they are elected to eternal life, in whom God does not foresee faith at all, much less antecedent faith. Let those elect infants be an example who die before by age they can believe, or persevere in faith. For what will never be future is not foreseen by God: since the object of foresight is something infallibly future.
pass_b_english: Now the syllogism. The Major — Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected to salvation — is stuffed with equivocations. Without which can mean: without which, foreseen as an antecedent condition, no one can be elected; or without which as a prepared, destined means no one can be elected. The first sense touches the cause but is manifestly false; the second does not even touch it, and still is not absolute truth. Some please God unto election to eternal life in whom God foresees no faith at all, still less antecedent faith — for example elect infants who die before they can believe or persevere. What will never be is not foreseen; foresight's object is something infallibly future.
source_text: Sed ipsum syllogismum ventilemus. Major propositio, Sine quo impossibile est placere Deo, sine eo impossibile est eligi quenquam ad salutem, tota farcta est aequivocationibus. Vocabula illa, sine quo, intelligi possunt dupliciter: sine quo praeviso et praeconsiderato ut antecedanea conditione nemo potest eligi ad salutem a Deo; vel, sine quo tanquam medio praeparato et destinato impossibile est eligi quenquam ad salutem. Priore sensu causam attingit, sed manifeste falsa est: Posteriore ne attingit quidem, et tamen non est absolutae veritatis. Nam quidem eatenus Deo placent, ut ad vitam aeternam eligantur, in quibus Deus non praevidet fidem omnino, nedum antecedaneam. Exemplo sint electi illi infantes qui moriuntur, priusquam per aetatem credere, aut in fide perseverare possint. Quod enim nunquam futurum est, a Deo non praevidetur: cum objectum praescientiae sit quiddam infallibiliter futurum.
